overview.title: 📖 Overview: When the Sin Itself Is Unknown
overview.subtitle: Keritot 19a–19b
overview.hebrewSource: אֲשֶׁר חָטָא בָּהּ – עַד שֶׁיִּוָּדַע לוֹ בַּמֶּה חָטָא
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf resolves lingering contradictions from the two-paths impurity case, distinguishing 'partial knowledge' from full knowledge and reconciling apparently conflicting statements from Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish by tracing them to different verses. A new mishna then raises the sharpest form of this problem: someone who certainly sinned, but cannot identify which of two forbidden acts he committed (forbidden fat or notar, his menstruating wife or his sister, Shabbat or Yom Kippur labor). Rabbi Eliezer holds he is liable regardless — either way he sinned — while Rabbi Yehoshua exempts him, since the Torah requires him to know specifically what he did. Rabbi Yosei, and separately Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri, each narrow exactly which version of this scenario the two disagree about. The daf closes with the special category of mit'asek — acting without any intent to sin at all — where the Gemara distinguishes cases of forbidden pleasure (still liable) from Shabbat labor (exempt, since it requires purposeful action).

slides.title: 🛤️ Partial Knowledge — Is It Knowledge?
slides.subtitle: Untangling self-contradictions in Rabbi Yoḥanan's and Reish Lakish's own statements

nodes.content: ❓ Someone walked path 1 (forgetting he'd walked it by the time he walked path 2), then entered the Temple — is that 'knowledge' of possible impurity?
⚖️ Dispute: the first tanna holds partial/forgotten knowledge still counts as knowledge; Rabbi Shimon holds it does not

🔄 Separately: why is one liable after purifying and re-entering with NO knowledge at all connecting the two entries? Reish Lakish: this baraita follows Rabbi Yishmael, who never requires 'knowledge at the outset.' Rabbi Yoḥanan: even the Rabbis agree HERE — the impurity verse's doubled language uniquely treats uncertain knowledge as full knowledge

🧩 Reconciling both Sages' apparent self-contradictions: Rabbi Yoḥanan limits his 'uncertain=full knowledge' rule to this specific impurity verse, not the rest of the Torah (which requires the ordinary phrase 'known to him'); Reish Lakish clarifies Rabbi Yishmael himself needs no such requirement at all

callout.label: Textual key:
callout.text: The impurity verse (Lev. 5:2) uniquely says 'it was concealed FROM him' — even uncertain awareness triggers liability there, unlike the general formula 'known TO him' used elsewhere in the Torah.

slides.title: 🤷 Either Way, You Sinned
slides.subtitle: A new mishna: total uncertainty about WHICH of two sins occurred
rows: Ate forbidden fat or notar, doesn't know which
Exempt — must know specifically what he ate
Relations with menstruating wife or sister, doesn't know which
Performed labor on Shabbat or Yom Kippur, doesn't know which day

callout.label: The textual fight:
callout.text: Rabbi Eliezer reads 'if his sin becomes known to him' (Lev. 4:23) as excluding only a mit'asek (accidental actor with no intent); Rabbi Yehoshua reads the same phrase as requiring he know specifically WHICH sin he committed before any offering applies.

slides.title: 🌆 Twilight and the Limits of the Dispute
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yosei: the twilight (Shabbat/Yom Kippur) case isn't even disputed

lines.speaker: R' Yosei
lines.text: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua never disagreed about the twilight case — both agree he's exempt, since I say: part of the labor happened today, part happened tomorrow, so neither day's threshold was actually crossed.

lines.speaker: Colleagues
lines.text: Test this: what if he lifted an object right at twilight and carried it between adjacent domains — fast enough that it couldn't span two days?

lines.speaker: R' Yosei
lines.text: 'You've been diligent examining me' — but I still hold firm: even that lifting can be conceptually split between the two days.

lines.speaker: Further challenge
lines.text: But doesn't Rabbi Eliezer elsewhere hold one liable for even a SINGLE added thread completing a weave — suggesting he'd count even a split act as complete?

lines.speaker: Rav Yosef's resolution
lines.text: Rabbi Yosei's version of Rabbi Eliezer's opinion must then read as requiring TWO added threads, not one — preserving the idea that a truly split act still needs its own full measure on each side.

callout.label: Key move:
callout.text: Rabbi Yosei doesn't deny the mishna's dispute — he relocates it to a different, more genuine case of true doubt.

slides.title: 🍇 One Category or Two?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri redraw where the dispute actually lies

boxes.title: Same category (one 'name') — no dispute, liable
items: E.g., picked grapes from one vine on Shabbat, unsure which vine — still clearly 'picking grapes,' a single recognized transgression
Both Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua agree he is liable

boxes.title: Two categories ('two names') — genuine dispute
items: E.g., picked fruit from a tree, unsure if it was a grapevine or a fig tree — two distinct categories of prohibited labor
Here Rabbi Eliezer says liable (sinned either way); Rabbi Yehoshua says exempt (doesn't know which)

callout.label: Rabbi Yehuda's addition:
callout.text: Even intending to pick figs and mistakenly picking grapes (a true mit'asek — wrong intent, wrong result) still falls under this same Eliezer/Yehoshua dispute, since he indeed intended SOME picking action.

slides.title: ✋ Acting Without Intent (Mit'asek)
slides.subtitle: Why does forbidden pleasure create liability while Shabbat labor requires real intent?

lines.speaker: Rav Naḥman (Shmuel)
lines.text: One who acts entirely unawares (mit'asek) — no intent to sin whatsoever — is still liable for forbidden fat or forbidden relations, since he derived pleasure regardless of intent. But for Shabbat labor, he's exempt, since the Torah requires 'purposeful labor' (melekhet maḥshevet).

lines.speaker: Rava's challenge
lines.text: But the mishna about circumcising the wrong baby (meant one, circumcised another) treats it as debated between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua — not a flat exemption!

lines.speaker: Rav Naḥman's answer
lines.text: That case involves inflicting a wound — normally exempt without constructive intent, but a wound is always liable regardless, so it's a special exception, not a real counterexample.

lines.speaker: Rav Yehuda's challenge
lines.text: What about intending to pick figs but picking grapes instead — surely THAT'S a Shabbat mit'asek case, yet it's disputed, not flatly exempt!

lines.speaker: Shmuel's resolution
lines.text: That case is different: he first intended grapes, then forgot and thought 'figs,' but his hand went to the grapes anyway — his ORIGINAL intent was actually fulfilled. Rabbi Eliezer counts that original intent as sufficient; Rabbi Yehoshua requires his final, conscious intent to match. A genuine mit'asek (zero relevant intent at any point) remains exempt for both.

callout.label: Bottom line:
callout.text: 'Intent' in halakha isn't binary — the Sages distinguish original intent, current intent, and pure accident, each triggering different liability rules.

summary.principle: Liability for an unwitting sin depends on precisely what kind of knowledge or intent is required — full knowledge versus partial, knowledge of the act's existence versus its specific identity, and genuine accident versus redirected intent — and these distinctions are drawn from the exact wording of each governing verse.

flowSteps.content: 🛤️ Partial or forgotten knowledge is tested against full knowledge in the two-paths impurity case
🤷 A new mishna asks: is 'you definitely sinned somehow' enough, or must you know the specific sin?
🌆 Rabbi Yosei relocates the real dispute away from the twilight case entirely

columns.content: 🍇 Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri limit the dispute to genuinely different categories of sin
✋ Mit'asek is liable for pleasure-based sins but exempt for Shabbat labor, which requires real intent

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: not all 'not knowing' is equal — halakha distinguishes doubt about identity, doubt about occurrence, and total absence of intent, each with its own rule

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yoḥanan's resolution, why does the impurity verse uniquely treat uncertain knowledge as equivalent to full knowledge, unlike the rest of the Torah?
o: Because impurity is always more severe than other sins
Because the impurity verse (Leviticus 5:2) uses the phrase 'it was concealed FROM him,' while the general Torah formula requires it to be 'known TO him'
Because impurity has no minimum measure
Because Rabbi Yoḥanan simply preferred a stricter ruling
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan derives the distinction from the specific wording of Leviticus 5:2 ('concealed from him'), which uniquely includes even uncertain awareness, unlike the standard formula elsewhere requiring definite knowledge.

quiz.q: In the new mishna's case of eating either forbidden fat or notar without knowing which, what is Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning for liability?
o: He believes uncertainty never matters
Either way, the person definitely sinned — one of the two prohibitions was certainly violated
He requires two witnesses regardless
He holds notar and forbidden fat are identical prohibitions
quiz.e: Rabbi Eliezer's argument is that regardless of which item was eaten, the person certainly transgressed one prohibition or the other, so he should be liable either way.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yosei, do Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua actually disagree about someone who performed labor during the twilight period between Shabbat and Yom Kippur, not knowing which day it was?
o: Yes, this is their central disagreement
No — Rabbi Yosei says they both agree he is exempt, since the labor can be understood as partly performed on each day
Yes, but only regarding Yom Kippur specifically
No, they both agree he is liable
quiz.e: Rabbi Yosei holds that Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua do not actually disagree about the twilight case — both agree the person is exempt, since the labor can be conceptually split between the two days, meaning no full measure was performed on either single day.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri, in which scenario do Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua actually disagree?
o: When the uncertainty involves two different categories ('two names') of prohibited labor, such as not knowing if fruit was picked from a grapevine or a fig tree
When the uncertainty involves the same category ('one name'), such as not knowing which of two vines the grapes came from
They never disagree about anything
Only when three or more categories are involved
quiz.e: Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri hold the dispute applies only when the uncertainty spans two distinct categories of prohibited labor; when it's the same category (one name), both agree he is liable.

quiz.q: According to Rav Naḥman (in the name of Shmuel), why is one who acts entirely without intent (mit'asek) still liable for eating forbidden fat or engaging in forbidden relations, but exempt for performing labor on Shabbat?
o: Because Shabbat labor is never prohibited without full intent

Because he derives pleasure from forbidden fat or forbidden relations regardless of intent, while the Torah requires purposeful, constructive intent (melekhet maḥshevet) specifically for Shabbat labor
Because forbidden fat carries no minimum measure
Because Shabbat labor always requires two witnesses
quiz.e: Rav Naḥman explains that pleasure-based prohibitions like forbidden fat or forbidden relations create liability regardless of intent, since the physical pleasure occurred regardless; Shabbat labor, by contrast, requires genuinely purposeful action (melekhet maḥshevet), so accidental labor without intent is exempt.
